title: ShapeFormer: Shapelet Transformer for Multivariate Time Series Classification

problem.claim: Multivariate time series classification requires learning representative characteristics across diverse real-world applications.

gap.claim: Existing transformer-based methods focus on generic features and overlook class-specific features, which can impair performance on imbalanced datasets or datasets whose classes differ in minor details.

contributions.claim: ShapeFormer combines class-specific and generic transformer modules to capture both feature types.
The class-specific module discovers class-discriminative subsequences and uses a Shapelet Filter to learn difference features between those shapelets and the input time series.
The generic module uses convolution filters, and transformer encoders in both modules capture correlations among their features.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors present ShapeFormer as a novel Shapelet Transformer for multivariate time series classification.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that shapelet difference features contain important class-specific information because they significantly distinguish a shapelet's class from other classes.
Experiments on 30 UEA multivariate time series classification datasets reportedly show that ShapeFormer achieves the highest accuracy ranking compared with state-of-the-art methods.

narrative_sequence.summary: MTSC is important, and transformer methods have recently achieved strong performance.
Generic-feature methods miss class-specific details, especially in imbalanced or closely patterned datasets.
ShapeFormer combines class-specific shapelet processing with generic feature extraction and transformer encoders.
The two transformer modules jointly exploit class-specific and generic features to improve classification.
The authors report the highest accuracy ranking on 30 UEA MTSC datasets.

source_observation.claim: Combining class-specific shapelet features with generic features is intended to address datasets where overall patterns are similar but discriminative details are local or class-specific.

interpretation.claim: Feature representations may benefit from explicitly separating shared structure from class-discriminative structure.

application.claim: For classification problems with class imbalance or subtle class differences, consider pairing generic representation learning with class-specific subsequence discovery.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish whether this design remains beneficial outside the evaluated UEA datasets or under different data conditions.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the 30 datasets, baselines, accuracy values, or statistical testing procedures.
The abstract does not describe computational cost, hyperparameters, ablations, or failure cases.
The abstract does not provide implementation or training details beyond the code-availability statement.
